title: Phu Thap Boek 2026 — Phetchabun's Peak, Sea of Fog & Camping
metaDesc: A guide to Phu Thap Boek, the highest point in Phetchabun, Thailand at 1,768m: terraced cabbage fields, morning sea of fog, camping spots, prices, how to get there, and the steep road you should know about before driving up.
keywords: Phu Thap Boek, Phetchabun sea of fog, Phu Thap Boek cabbage fields, Phu Thap Boek camping, Phu Thap Boek road
h1:
Phu Thap Boek
The Highest Point in Phetchabun
intro: Phu Thap Boek is the highest mountain in Phetchabun, sitting at around 1,768 meters above sea level. People come up to sleep over and wait for the first light, when a sea of fog drifts through the terraced green cabbage fields stacked all the way down the valley. It stays cold for most of the year, and the views are striking enough to earn it the nickname "stars on the ground." But before you get there, there's a steep road you'll want to understand first.

blocks.html: Phu Thap Boek sits in Lom Kao district, right on the edge of Dan Sai in Loei province. It's home to the Hmong village of Thap Boek, where the highland community has farmed cabbage on the mountain slopes for generations. The image that sticks with people is rows of green cabbage stacked in tiers down the steep slope, with a sea of fog filling the valley on mornings when the weather plays along. Most visitors stay one night to catch the morning light, because the best views only happen between about 5 and 7 a.m.

blocks.text: Why go up Phu Thap Boek

blocks.html: The main reason is the altitude. At nearly 1,800 meters, Phu Thap Boek is noticeably colder than Khao Kho, which sits lower down. In winter the temperature regularly drops to single digits, and it's one of the better spots in Phetchabun for catching a thick sea of fog, since on many mornings you're standing above the cloud layer.

items: The province's highest point — the Phu Thap Boek summit sign at 1,768 meters is the check-in spot where people line up for photos.
Terraced cabbage fields — green cabbage plots stepping down the slope, a sight that's hard to find anywhere else in Thailand.
Morning sea of fog — on a clear morning the fog floods the valley until it feels like you're standing above the sea.
Stars on the ground — at night, looking down at the village lights twinkling below feels like stars fell and piled up on the earth.

items.label: Day trips from Phetchabun
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.html: Phu Thap Boek works almost year-round, but each season gives you a different picture. Pick based on what you want most, whether that's a thick sea of fog or fields fully green with cabbage.

items: November–January — coldest, thickest fog, and the most crowded. Rooms fill up fast, so book ahead.
Late rainy season, August–October — fresh green, and the fog rolls in often thanks to the high humidity, but expect on-and-off rain and slippery roads.
May–July — the cabbage is fully grown, there are fewer people, room rates are cheaper, and the weather is pleasant.

blocks.title: About the sea of fog
blocks.html: The fog isn't a sure thing every morning. It depends on the humidity and a clear sky. Mornings after overnight rain give you the best odds. Set an alarm for 5:30 a.m. and go stand at the viewpoint. If there's no fog that morning, that's just part of the gamble. No one can guarantee it.

items.name: Phu Thap Boek summit, 1,768 m
items.blurb: The highest point has a sign for photos and views all around. Early in the morning it gets packed with people waiting for first light and the sea of fog.

items.name: Pha Hua Sing (Lion's Head Cliff)
items.blurb: A cliff shaped a bit like a lion's head, with views nearly all around. Fewer people make it out here, so it's quieter than the main summit. It's just a short walk in from the parking area.

items.name: Terraced cabbage fields
items.blurb: The photo spot for the tiered green fields that define Phu Thap Boek. They look best in the morning when the light comes in low and a thin haze still lingers.

blocks.text: Camping and lodging: what does it cost

blocks.html: Places to stay on Phu Thap Boek range from the community camping grounds run by the Thap Boek village enterprise to cabins and domes with private bathrooms. The prices below are the going rates we found from local operators, meant as a rough guide. They can shift with the season and the spot you choose.

items.name: Bring your own tent (community ground)
items.blurb: Pitch your own tent and pay a per-person site fee. You get the cabbage-field and sea-of-fog views at the cheapest rate, ideal for campers who have all their own gear.

items.name: Cliffside camping ground (walk in)
items.blurb: An open-view ground right along the cliff edge. Many spots have no electricity, so bring a flashlight and a power bank. Wake up to fog right outside your tent.

items.name: Rent a bare tent
items.blurb: No gear? You can rent a bare tent from a local operator and bring your own bedding. Good for anyone who doesn't want to haul a tent up the mountain.

items.name: Tent with bedding for 4
items.blurb: A tent that comes with mattresses and warm blankets, sleeping about four. Show up and go straight to bed, nothing to prepare.

items.name: Cabin with private bathroom
items.blurb: A small cabin with its own bathroom, warmer than sleeping in a tent. Good for anyone who'd rather not risk the deep cold in the middle of the night.

items.name: Dome tent with private bathroom
items.blurb: A glamping dome with its own bathroom. You get the feel of sleeping in a tent with resort-style convenience. It's the top option on the community ground.

blocks.title: Before you book
blocks.html: In winter the lodging up here fills up fast, especially on long weekends, so book several weeks ahead. And ask clearly whether the spot has electricity, a bathroom, and hot water, because many camping grounds don't. Always pack a heavy jacket, gloves, and a beanie.

blocks.text: Getting there and the steep road

blocks.html: The most convenient way is to drive your own car or rent one. From Bangkok, take Highway 21 the whole way into Phetchabun. This stretch is wide and easy to drive. Turn off into Lom Kao and then climb up to Phu Thap Boek. The part to watch is the final stretch before the summit, which is one of the steepest and most winding mountain roads in Thailand.

items: It really is steep — the last stretch before the village is very steep. An underpowered or fully loaded car may struggle, and you'll need low gear to drag it up.
Automatic transmission — it can make it, but lock it into low gear (L or 1–2) both going up and coming down. Don't let the car coast and rely on the brakes alone.
The way down matters more than the way up — use low gear to brake with the engine. Don't ride the brakes the whole way, or they'll overheat, fade, and stop holding.
New drivers — if you're not confident on steep climbs, locals run songthaews and pickups for the final stretch up to the summit, paid per trip. It's safer than forcing the drive yourself.

blocks.title: Check your car before heading up
blocks.html: Before climbing, make sure your brake pads and tires are in good shape. Fill up the tank in Lom Kao, since fuel stations are scarce up top. If it's raining the road gets especially slick, so take it slow. There's no need to rush.

Up on the mountain there's the Thap Boek Hmong market, selling fresh cold-climate vegetables, seasonal strawberries, pickled fruit, fruit wine, and Hmong-pattern jackets as souvenirs. For a warm meal, there are made-to-order shops and local noodle stalls scattered around the lodging areas. Slurping something hot on a freezing morning hits just right.

items: Cold-climate vegetables — cabbage and lettuce fresh from the fields, cheaper than in town, and you can take them home.
Seasonal strawberries — available from late in the year into early the next, both fresh and pickled or made into jam, a popular souvenir.
Something warm in the morning — noodles, rice porridge, and hot coffee are easy to find at shops near the camping grounds, and help you fight the cold.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Up the mountain, set up camp, wait for sunset

items.activity: Reach Lom Kao, fill up the tank, have lunch, and check the car before climbing.
items.note: Fuel is scarce up top, so fill up first.

items.activity: Drive up Phu Thap Boek. The final stretch is steep and winding, so use low gear and take it slow.
items.note: If you're not confident, park below and take a local songthaew up.

items.activity: Check in / set up your tent, wander the cabbage fields, and photograph the terraced rows.
items.note: Pick an open-view spot to wait for the morning light.

items.activity: Watch the sunset at the viewpoint, walk the Hmong market for souvenirs, and find something warm to eat.
items.note: It gets very cold at night, so pack a heavy jacket.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Morning sea of fog, then down the mountain

items.activity: Get up and stand by at the viewpoint, hoping for the sea of fog and first light.
items.note: Wear a heavy jacket, gloves, and a beanie.

items.activity: Photograph the cabbage fields with the thin haze in the low light, and have a hot breakfast.
items.note: This is the prettiest light of the day.

items.activity: Pack up, check out, and head down using low gear to brake with the engine, without riding the brakes.
items.note: The way down needs more care than the way up.

items.activity: Stop by Khao Kho or Wat Pha Sorn Kaew on the way back.
items.note: Khao Kho is nearby and easy to add to the trip.

blocks.text: Things to know before you go

items: It's genuinely cold — night and morning temperatures are much lower than in town, so always pack a heavy jacket, gloves, and a hat.
Phone signal — it's weak in some spots, so save offline maps and your lodging location before heading up.
Cash — many shops and lodgings on the mountain take cash, so bring enough.
Pack out your trash — this is a community area and the villagers' farmland, so carry your trash back down to help keep the view for the next generation.

faq.q: How high is Phu Thap Boek?
faq.a: The Phu Thap Boek summit is around 1,768 meters above sea level, the highest point in Phetchabun province and higher than the viewpoints on Khao Kho, which is why it's colder and more likely to have a sea of fog.

faq.q: Can I drive a sedan or an automatic up Phu Thap Boek?
faq.a: You can, but the final stretch before the summit is very steep and winding, so lock it into low gear both up and down. An underpowered or fully loaded car may struggle. If you're not confident, locals run songthaews for the final stretch up to the summit.

faq.q: How much does camping at Phu Thap Boek cost?
faq.a: If you bring your own tent, the site fee is around 100 THB per person. A bare tent rents for around 500 THB, and a tent with bedding that sleeps about four is around 900 THB. Cabins and domes with private bathrooms start at around 1,500–2,500 THB. Rates shift with the season.

faq.q: When is it easiest to catch the sea of fog at Phu Thap Boek?
faq.a: November to January is the coldest with the thickest fog. The late rainy season from August to October also brings fog often thanks to the high humidity. Mornings after overnight rain give you the best odds, though no one can guarantee it every morning.

faq.q: How are Phu Thap Boek and Khao Kho different?
faq.a: Phu Thap Boek is higher and colder, with views of cabbage fields and the sea of fog, but the road is steeper. Khao Kho sits lower, is easier to reach, and has more cafes and attractions. The two are close together, so you can visit both on one trip.
